During this pelagic larval phase, individuals are highly vulnerable to predation, and the small size at hatching necessitates a high initial investment in larval numbers to offset substantial early-life mortality, a common ecological trade-off observed among coral reef teleosts.

The transition from juvenile to adult is marked not only by the onset of reproductive capability but also by a distinct shift in coloration and social behavior, with mature males establishing dominance hierarchies on the reef.

The maximum recorded body size for Scarus altipinnis, based on extensive underwater visual census data and spear-fishing collections, is 60 cm [Li = 60 cm] in total length.
